**My Lai Massacre**
The March 1968 killing of hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians by U.S. soldiers of Charlie Company in the hamlet of My Lai (codenamed "Pinkville"), in the Son Tinh district. Villagers were herded into ditches and shot. Lieutenant William Calley was the only soldier convicted. Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson tried to stop the killing, Ronald Ridenhour's letters prompted an investigation, and journalist Seymour Hersh exposed the story. Army photographer Ronald Haeberle's photo of the bodies became the antiwar poster "And babies."

**Tet Offensive**
A massive surprise attack by the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese Army launched in January 1968 during a truce for Tet, the Lunar New Year. Attackers struck cities across South Vietnam, briefly breached the U.S. embassy compound in Saigon, and fought a long urban battle in Hue. Although it was a military defeat for the communists, it shattered American public confidence in the war and in General William Westmoreland, the U.S. commander, who was replaced by Creighton Abrams.

**Siege of Khe Sanh**
A siege of U.S. Marines and allied forces at a mountain combat base in northwestern South Vietnam from January to April 1968, around the time of the Tet Offensive. Some historians believe it was meant partly to distract U.S. attention from the coming attacks on the cities.

**Gulf of Tonkin incident**
In August 1964 the destroyer USS Maddox reported attacks by North Vietnamese patrol boats in the Gulf of Tonkin; a second reported attack probably never happened. Congress responded with the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which gave President Lyndon Johnson broad power to escalate U.S. military involvement in Vietnam.

**Agent Orange and Operation Ranch Hand**
Agent Orange was a dioxin-contaminated herbicide that Operation Ranch Hand sprayed from C-123 aircraft to strip jungle cover and destroy crops, including along supply trails. Manufacturers included Monsanto and Dow Chemical, and Ranch Hand crews used the parody motto "Only you can prevent a forest." It caused lasting health problems in Vietnam and among veterans. Napalm, an incendiary jelly, was also widely used.

**Kent State shootings**
On May 4, 1970, Ohio National Guardsmen fired on students protesting Richard Nixon's invasion of Cambodia at Kent State University, killing four. A famous photo shows 14-year-old runaway Mary Ann Vecchio kneeling and screaming over the body of a slain student.

**Strategic Hamlet Program**
A program begun in 1962 by South Vietnam's government, with U.S. support, to move rural peasants into fortified villages and cut them off from communist guerrillas. It was modeled on British resettlement camps from the Malayan Emergency. It was resented and largely failed.

**Tinker v. Des Moines**
A 1969 Supreme Court case in which the Court ruled that Iowa students who wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War were exercising protected free speech. In the Court's words, students do not "shed their constitutional rights... at the schoolhouse gate."

**Fall of Saigon and Operation Frequent Wind**
On April 30, 1975, North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon, the South Vietnamese capital (later renamed Ho Chi Minh City), ending the war after Le Duan's Spring Offensive. South Vietnam's last president, Duong Van Minh, surrendered. Irving Berlin's "White Christmas" played on Armed Forces Radio as the signal to begin Operation Frequent Wind, the helicopter evacuation of Americans and Vietnamese. A famous photo shows people climbing a ladder to a helicopter on a Saigon rooftop. Vietnam now celebrates April 30 as a national holiday.

**Thich Quang Duc and Ngo Dinh Diem**
In 1963 the Buddhist monk Thich Quang Duc burned himself to death in a Saigon street to protest persecution of Buddhists by South Vietnam's Catholic president Ngo Dinh Diem. Malcolm Browne's photograph of the burning monk, with his car's hood open behind him, became world famous. The Buddhist crisis prompted U.S. fact-finding missions (Krulak–Mendenhall, then McNamara–Taylor), and Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup in November 1963.

**Pentagon Papers**
A secret Defense Department history of U.S. decision-making in Vietnam, leaked in 1971 by military analyst Daniel Ellsberg to The New York Times and The Washington Post. Senator Mike Gravel read portions into the record, and the 2017 film The Post depicts their publication.

**Ho Chi Minh Trail**
A network of roads and paths through Laos and Cambodia that North Vietnam used to supply Viet Cong guerrillas in the South. It was built and run by a North Vietnamese unit called Group 559. The U.S. bombed it, sprayed it with herbicides, and laid an "electronic fence" of sensors along it, which enemy soldiers reportedly fooled with buckets of urine.

**Operation Rolling Thunder**
A long U.S. aerial bombing campaign against North Vietnam from 1965 to 1968. It was restricted in its targets and meant to pressure Hanoi gradually and choke off supplies to the South.

**Antiwar protests and the draft**
Opposition to the war took many forms, including burning draft cards, fleeing to Canada to "dodge" the draft, the 1967 March on the Pentagon (where Abbie Hoffman tried to "levitate" the building and Norman Mailer was arrested), and the Catonsville Nine, led by the priests Daniel and Philip Berrigan, who burned draft files. Boxer Muhammad Ali refused induction. Nixon appealed to the "silent majority" against protesters, and pro-war construction workers attacked protesters in the 1970 Hard Hat Riot.

**Paris Peace Accords**
The 1973 agreement that ended direct U.S. military involvement in Vietnam. Henry Kissinger and North Vietnam's Le Duc Tho were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for negotiating it, and Le Duc Tho declined his share. Earlier, in 1968, Anna Chennault allegedly worked to stall peace talks on behalf of Richard Nixon's presidential campaign.
